title: Maximizing AI Factory Performance per Watt with NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA's DSX MaxLPS system (dynamic power software, workload power profiles, and 45C liquid cooling) reclaims power stranded by static rack provisioning, delivering up to 40% more Rubin GPU capacity and 1.3-1.5x performance-per-watt within a fixed power envelope — reframing NVIDIA's product pitch around power-constrained AI factories rather than raw chip count, with direct implications for the datacenter power buildout bottleneck.

themes.theme: AI factories are power-constrained, not chip-constrained

insights.claim: The article's central framing is that AI factories are power-constrained industrial systems, so the relevant question is no longer how many GPUs fit in a data center but how much AI output each available megawatt can deliver, making performance-per-watt the key efficiency metric for AI inference workloads.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: This reframes the AI infrastructure investment thesis: capex-constrained buildouts are shifting from 'buy more GPUs' to 'extract more useful compute per megawatt of grid power,' which favors vendors (like NVIDIA) that sell power-optimization software/hardware alongside chips, and implies grid power access is becoming the binding constraint on AI scaling.
insights.quote: AI factories are power-constrained industrial systems. The question is no longer how many GPUs fit in a data center, but how much AI output each available megawatt can deliver.

insights.claim: In one representative power-budget view examined by NVIDIA for a 100 MW AI factory, only about 60% of delivered site power (60 MW) is actually allocated to AI-load compute, with 20 MW lost to facility overhead, 10 MW to rack losses, and 10 MW unavailable due to operational inefficiency during failures, restarts, and checkpointing.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified power-budget waterfall (40% of grid power never reaches compute) gives investors a benchmark to sanity-check disclosed or implied PUE/efficiency claims from hyperscalers and datacenter operators — a large efficiency gap represents both risk (wasted capex) and opportunity (software that reclaims it).
insights.locator: Figure 1 / power-budget waterfall for a 100 MW AI factory

insights.claim: Static rack provisioning — the traditional approach of allocating maximum power draw per rack to meet worst-case peak demand — treats each rack as an isolated power island, so an isolated rack provisioned with excess power cannot lend that unused headroom to a neighboring rack that could turn it into tokens.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Identifies a structural, industry-wide inefficiency (not NVIDIA-specific) in how data centers have historically been designed, implying a broad addressable market for dynamic power management software across all AI datacenter operators, not just NVIDIA's own installed base.
insights.quote: An isolated rack provisioned with excess power cannot lend that unused power to a neighbor that could turn it into tokens.
insights.locator: Why static rack provisioning strands power

themes.theme: NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS: dynamic power allocation product

insights.claim: NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS ('Maximum Land Power Shell') is a suite of chip, thermal, system, and software technologies designed to maximize AI factory throughput within a fixed power budget by optimizing three layers: dynamic power allocation, advanced performance-per-watt software techniques, and 45C thermal/site design.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Defines a new NVIDIA product category spanning silicon, cooling, and software — a bundled systems sale (not just GPUs) that could raise NVIDIA's revenue capture per datacenter deployment and deepen platform lock-in versus commodity GPU competitors.
insights.locator: NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS is a suite of chip, thermal, system, and software technologies

insights.claim: Dynamic Power Software (DPS), currently in Developer Preview, is a power management system that models data center topology from the utility level down to racks, nodes, and GPUs, continuously comparing allocated power against actual consumption and making unused headroom available to other GPUs/racks in the same managed group in real time.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: DPS being in Developer Preview (not GA) signals this is an early-stage but strategically important product to track for adoption timing and future revenue contribution — worth monitoring for GA announcement and hyperscaler adoption.
insights.locator: How does NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS dynamic power allocation work?

insights.claim: In an illustrative comparison, static power provisioning strands 170 kW of power while MaxLPS dynamic provisioning reclaims that headroom, enabling an additional rack deployment within the same fixed 540 kW site power budget.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: A concrete illustrative ratio (170kW reclaimed out of 540kW budget, roughly 31%) that investors can use to estimate potential capacity uplift from software alone, without new power contracts or land — relevant to how fast operators can scale AI capacity given grid interconnection delays.
insights.locator: Figure 3 / static vs MaxLPS dynamic provisioning

insights.claim: DSX Exchange, also in Developer Preview, is an open-source IT/OT event bus connecting DPS and other DSX services to building management systems, electrical power monitoring, cooling infrastructure, grid interfaces, and compute schedulers; MaxLPS does not require DSX Exchange to function but the integration exposes additional signals like seasonal cooling headroom for DPS to act on.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: An open-source event bus strategy suggests NVIDIA is trying to become the integration standard connecting AI compute scheduling with physical facility/grid systems — a platform land-grab into building/grid operations technology (OT), an adjacent market to its core GPU business.
insights.locator: DSX Exchange is an open source event bus for AI factory operations

insights.claim: For NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 AI factories, NVIDIA projects MaxLPS combined with data center power planning can enable up to 40% more Rubin GPU capacity within the same power budget.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: A 40% capacity uplift claim for NVIDIA's next-gen Rubin platform is a major go-to-market number for NVIDIA's upcoming product cycle — a headline metric likely to be repeated in sales conversations with hyperscalers and should be tracked against real-world validated results as Rubin ships.
insights.locator: For NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 AI factories, NVIDIA projects that MaxLPS

insights.claim: In representative inference workload testing (Vera Rubin NVL72 with DeepSeek-R1; GB200 NVL72 with Kimi-K2.5), MaxLPS reduced provisioned rack power from 125kW to 90kW on GB200 NVL72 (39% more racks) and from 136kW to 101kW on Vera Rubin NVL72 (35% more racks) within the same power envelope while preserving throughput; performance per watt improved ~1.5x on GB200 NVL72 and 1.3-1.4x on Vera Rubin NVL72.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: These are the article's hardest, most specific validated numbers (not just projections) — a directly citable data point for modeling datacenter capex efficiency gains, and notably it uses DeepSeek and Moonshot's Kimi as benchmark workloads, indicating those models are now standard datacenter test workloads alongside NVIDIA's own stack.

insights.claim: MaxLPS includes optimized Workload Profile Power Solutions (WPPS) for common operating modes (inference, training, memory-bound, compute-bound), applied via the Application Performance and Power Manager (APPM), while NVIDIA Dynamo can further optimize inter-rack performance and power behavior for inference services — the stated principle is aligning GPU configuration, application behavior, and serving topology to raise fleet-wide output per watt.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Shows NVIDIA integrating power management with its inference-serving stack (Dynamo), extending the moat beyond hardware into the full serving/power software stack that competitors would need to replicate end-to-end.
insights.locator: Maxlps techniques for advanced performance per watt

themes.theme: 45C liquid cooling and facility design implications

insights.claim: Vera Rubin NVL72 racks are designed for 45C liquid-cooling inlet operation; warmer coolant lets facilities rely more often on 'free cooling' (outside air/water with minimal mechanical chilling), reducing reliance on energy-intensive chillers or water-intensive adiabatic coolers and lowering average annual power usage effectiveness (PUE).
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Higher rated inlet temperatures is a hardware-level design choice with direct capex/opex consequences for datacenter builders — signals NVIDIA is engineering silicon/rack thermal tolerance specifically to reduce facility cooling costs, a competitive differentiator versus chips requiring colder cooling.
insights.locator: Why is 45 C liquid cooling important?

insights.claim: Heat rejection systems are typically sized for worst-case scenarios, but many sites require far less chiller compressor power under typical conditions; if electrical distribution, dry coolers, and controls are sized for that flexibility, power budgeted for the worst-hour cooling load becomes available to compute during much of the year.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Identifies a second, independent source of stranded capacity (cooling overprovisioning, distinct from rack power overprovisioning) — implies further efficiency upside beyond the headline 40% GPU capacity number if facilities are designed for this flexibility from the start.
insights.locator: Recovering that cooling power for compute is a facilities design problem

insights.claim: Traditional reactive PID (proportional-integral-derivative) control of coolant distribution units is common but responds only after sensors detect a deviation; because large AI factories create fast, synchronized thermal load changes, operators often run the loop colder than necessary to preserve margin, wasting cooling power that could otherwise support compute.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Calls out an industry-standard control approach (PID) as suboptimal for AI workloads specifically, opening the door for predictive/agentic cooling control as a differentiated software sale.
insights.locator: Operating the technology cooling system loop efficiently

insights.claim: Agentic control systems for cooling, including work by Phaidra, use power telemetry and learned control policies to anticipate thermal behavior rather than reacting after the fact, though a rack with 45C thermal efficiency does not require agentic control to operate — agentic control is described as an optimization layered on top of, not required by, the base hardware/facility design.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Names a specific third-party partner (Phaidra) in NVIDIA's cooling-optimization ecosystem — a concrete signal of NVIDIA's partner strategy for AI-driven facility operations, useful for tracking competitive/partnership dynamics in the datacenter-cooling software space.
insights.locator: Operating the technology cooling system loop efficiently

insights.claim: MaxLPS infrastructure design starts from a fixed gross facility power envelope and works inward to set the long-term infrastructure target (power, cooling, space, network) and the maximum GPU rack-position count the site can ultimately support, while Day 1 deployment can start below that limit — early workloads skewed toward training/post-training draw more power per rack and thus support fewer initial racks than the eventual inference-heavy steady state.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: Implies AI datacenters should be designed upfront for a future inference-heavy workload mix even if early deployment is training-heavy, avoiding costly retrofits later — a planning framework relevant to how much capex flexibility operators should build in from day one, and a signal that NVIDIA expects training-to-inference workload mix shift over facility lifecycles.
insights.locator: How to size an AI factory site for MaxLPS

insights.claim: NVIDIA advises operators to retrofit or design for MaxLPS at the site level even before deploying every rack on Day 1, and to engage NVIDIA early to validate 45C thermal design, rack-position optionality, and power distribution flexibility before infrastructure decisions are fixed, since physical infrastructure is difficult to change once built.
insights.speaker: Sarah McKenney
insights.so_what: This is effectively a sales/engagement call-to-action embedded in technical content — signals NVIDIA is positioning itself as an early-stage design partner for hyperscaler/neocloud datacenter buildouts, extending its commercial relationship upstream into facilities planning, well before GPU purchase orders.
insights.quote: Physical infrastructure is difficult to change once built.
